speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTERNATIONAL COFFEE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In reply to a question of mine yesterday it was indicated that the retail price of coffee in Canada had increased by some 25 per cent to 30 per cent in line with the international coffee agreement. Is Canada satisfied with this agreement, or is some thought being given to protecting coffee drinkers by seeking amendments to it?
Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, I happen to have been the chairman of the international coffee conference at which the present coffee agreement was negotiated. At that time coffee prices were at very low levels, lower than at any time in the past decade, and it was agreed by the then Canadian government and by all the other countries of the world that this was causing human hardship and was interfering with the development of countries that produce and export coffee.
When the agreement came into effect in July, 1963 prices were, as I say, at these very low levels. Shortly thereafter there was a very serious drought in Brazil, which was the main cause for the increase in prices. Indeed, the increase had very little to do with the international coffee agreement. Then, when these prices rose very sharply as a result of the change in the supply situation, the members subscribing to the coffee agreement acted quickly to increase the permissible supplies of coffee being marketed under the agreement, with the result that coffee prices came down from their high point.
In answer specifically to the question as to whether Canada is satisfied with the operation of the agreement, I would say that this agreement can be improved; and it can be improved, I think, for the benefit of both consumers and producers. I would urge upon my hon. friend who asked this question that it is very much in the interests of all of us,
Inquiries of the Ministry including the consumers of Canada, that there should be reasonable prices for coffee, just as there should be reasonable prices for wheat.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTERNATIONAL COFFEE AGREEMENT
speechtext: And turkeys.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTERNATIONAL COFFEE AGREEMENT

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTERNATIONAL COFFEE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I know this. I know the reluctance there has been in the United States for many years to agree to any international commodity agreement. This has been a standing difficulty, but I do hope this agreement will be ratified.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, September 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hays for the second reading of Bill No. C-121, to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture gave us some further information concerning the general outline of the bill we are discussing, which has to do with loans to farm machinery syndicates. This was done because on this side of the house many questions were asked at the resolution stage pertaining to the background of the legislation. When the minister was pressed at the resolution stage he stated that in the terms of the bill itself, and the explanations that would follow, answers would be found to these many pertinent questions.
Although the parliamentary secretary did comply with our requests to a degree, there still remain many broad questions with respect to the principles of the bill about which we would like to be satisfied. After having had the opportunity to read the bill I must say that personally I am very disappointed. I am of the opinion that the measure may indeed be of some help to a few large farm complexes throughout the country, but in its application it will do very little to help the ordinary farmer who seems to be in difficulty today.
The approach of the government in the bill, as with any other farm legislation or policy that has been introduced by the government, seems to follow one particular course, to provide further funds by way of credit for our farmers who, if they take advantage of it, find themselves deeper and deeper in debt. In my opinion this in no way attacks the basic problem of farming today because farmers do not want to be in debt. They do not want too much additional credit. What they want is an attempt by the government

Farm Machinery
either to increase their incomes or decrease their operating expenses in order to give them the necessary capital to finance themselves. It is my honest opinion that the bill, as in the case of other legislative applications of policy by the government, does nothing to attack these basic problems facing agriculture today. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and the parliamentary secretary spoke about the 80 per cent of the cost that the loan would cover and the 20 per cent that would have to be put up by the individuals joining such a syndicate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would hope that in the course of a few minutes this afternoon I could ask the parliamentary secretary or the minister some of the questions that must be going through the minds of farmers today who are aware of this legislation. I hope that before we get into the committee stage on this bill the parliamentary secretary might provide the answers to these questions, which I am sure must be troubling these farmers. We have heard about this 80 per cent-20 per cent basis, but what the farmers will want to know is how this 20 per cent is going to be broken up amongst the members of the syndicate. Is each member of the syndicate to be assessed an equal amount of this equity or is there to be a disparity amongst the members who join? Can one member put up 10 per cent and the other three members provide the other 10 per cent or must they all assume an equal amount of this liability? This is one of the questions farmers are asking today.
, We understand from the parliamentary secretary that each member will be allowed to borrow up to $15,000, and that there will be a maximum of $100,000 for the syndicate. We find the same regulation applying to farm improvement loans, and we wonder just what difference there will be. The parliamentary secretary stated this will in no way jeopardize the ability of farmers to borrow under the farm improvement loans legislation. Here again a question arises. If a farmer has borrowed $15,000 under the farm improvement loans legislation and has used his assets as collateral, will these same assets not be necessary for collateral for a farm machinery loan? Certainly the parliamentary secretary would not, I believe, contend that the same amount of capital can be used as collateral for both of these loans.
Then there is the seven year limit. If $100,000 is borrowed and the interest rate is the prevailing rate, plus 1 per cent for

the cost of operation, it could mean 6 per cent spread over seven years. If there are five or six participants in this syndicate it would mean the repayment would amount to perhaps $6,000 per member per year, which is quite an obligation to be undertaken by a farmer.
There is another question that is bothering farmers today. What effect will this measure have on private enterprise? Throughout Canada today there are machine agents who are providing pools of machinery and making equipment available to their neighbours and farmers in the area, and charging operation costs on a custom basis. In what position does this measure place these men? There is a provision in this legislation to the effect that every member of a syndicate does not have to be a full time farmer. This has caused a lot of worry amongst members of the opposition because they believe it will lead to integration and we shall see big business come into the field to take over the tools necessary to do farm work. I am sure farmers all across this country would like to see these loans strictly limited to farmers. Farmers have a great deal of suspicion about pouring money into the hands of individuals not engaged in farm work who may be induced to come into the field, because in many cases this does not promote the best interests of the farmers themselves.
The parliamentary secretary spoke about general provisions. Farmers have found as a result of bitter experience that it is always a simple matter for them to obtain money from the various farm corporations, provided they have the necessary security. It is always a simple matter to contract into these things. When we are talking about $100,000, the farmers want to know how they contract out of something like this if it does not meet with their approval or does not live up to their expectations. The parliamentary secretary has stated that general provisions would be enacted for adding new members, to cover the death or insolvency of a member and for the dissolution of the syndicate. These are very general terms, Mr. Speaker, and general terms do not mean very much to a farmer in connection with an undertaking of this size.
We would like the government, if it is in a position to do so, to elaborate on these general provisions and to indicate what machinery they envisage might be set up to take care of this very important part of this measure. The farmers want to know what

happens if a partner becomes bankrupt. Where do we stand then? What happens if one of the partners should die? Am I saddled with that part of the obligation? If I want to get out of this syndicate, how do I get out or can I get out? How much of the obligation am I going to be forced to assume to get out of the syndicate? What factors are taken into consideration? What about the devaluation of the machinery the syndicate has purchased? These are some of the questions farmers are asking themselves today. Farmers are businessmen, Mr. Speaker, and they want to look at this measure strictly as businessmen. I feel that they are right in asking these questions.
The next question is, how do we arrive at the type of machinery we are going to buy? What happens if there is a disagreement amongst the members of the syndicate as to the type of machinery we want to buy? The members might agree on the type of machine, but there may be a difference of opinion over the company that is to furnish this machine. There are many machine companies today making machinery which is used for the same purpose but which may be slightly different. The farmers want to know how these matters are going to be decided. Are we going to have the members of the syndicate making all these decisions, or will the syndicate be subjected to a mass of rules and regulations relating to each of these difficulties that might arise? The farmers want to know exactly what they are going to get into. In my opinion it is not sufficient to state there will be general provisions.
It is stated that before a syndicate is formed the members will be required to make arrangements regarding shares, regarding repairs, operating costs, storage and allocation of priority for use of the machine. Now, Mr. Speaker, what is meant by "make arrangements"? Is it going to be stated that before a syndicate is brought into being you must form a board of directors, that you must have bylaws? Is it to be a closed corporation? What are the operating methods by which these arrangements are going to be made? Who makes these arrangements? Who decides what machinery shall be bought? Who decides the type of machinery that shall be bought? What happens when a new member is brought into the syndicate? How is he treated? What part of the obligation does he assume? Does he have to contribute toward the full cost of the machinery or the depreciated value of the machinery? These are the questions we
Farm Machinery
would like to have answered before we deal with this bill clause by clause.
We hear that a number of persons may join a syndicate. This poses another problem in connection with farm credit. Farmers do not want to tie up all their credit in farm machinery. They have to have credit for fertilizers, for livestock and for seed. If I understand this bill correctly, when a person joins the syndicate he must sign a promissory note, and he must assume the entire obligation because, as I understand it, the obligation is assumed jointly and severally. Farmers want to know if they borrow $15,000 individually and the syndicate borrows $100,000, is the credit of a farmer assessed for the entire $100,000? When the farmer goes to a bank to borrow additional funds and this promissory note is disclosed, does this work against his credit to the full extent of $100,000? If such is the case, then there are hundreds of thousands of farmers whose credit would be absolutely at an end if they belonged to a syndicate operated under such an arrangement.
We are certainly not going to oppose this bill in its entirety. We are not going to oppose the principle of the bill, because we are of the opinion that if there is anything at all that will help the farmers we will support it, and if the farmers can use further credit we shall support the provision of it. If farmers can obtain and use better equipment, then that is all to the good; but I fear this bill will not accomplish what the government hopes it can, because I do not think the farmers will utilize this credit.
It will probably be businessmen who hope to invest money and earn a living that way, who will use the provisions of this bill. There may be large farm complexes which will take advantage of it, but these are few in number; and I believe that after the bill has been in operation for a few years the government will find it is a very poor one indeed. The government will find that it is not attacking the basic farm problems, that it is window dressing, and that it fails to meet basic farm needs.
It is my opinion that the provision of more credit to farmers at this stage is not the answer to farm problems. Some attempt must be made to assess and combat the two basic problems facing farmers today, which are lack of gross income and the increase in operating expenses. The gap is narrowing every year and farmers are finding it increasingly difficult to cope with these problems. All the government is doing through the

Farm Machinery
Farm Credit Corporation, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and now through this farm machinery syndicate bill is offering greater and greater credit to farmers which, for the most part, will put them more and more in debt, unless something is done to attack the basic problems of agriculture. The farmers of Quebec, Ontario, the maritimes, the west and B.C. know what the problems are. They have made representations to the government on their basic problems, and it is my opinion that a measure such as this will not in any way alleviate the basic problems they are facing.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to make a few brief observations on this somewhat unusual bill to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates, the exact purpose of which is still somewhat of a mystery to the members of the house.
Before I proceed I should explain that I have been a farmer all my life, but in contrast to the many well-to-do farmers we find in the ranks of the Progressive Conservative party I have been associated more with the axe, the grub hoe and the walking plow throughout my life.

speechtext: You are an agricultural plutocrat.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
However, I am just as interested in this bill as if I were the owner of a very large farm and had a large amount of equipment. I might say, Mr. Speaker, as my leader previously said, that we support the apparent principle of the bill, which even at this time is somewhat obscure, but the over-all general intention appears to be good. However, we shall have to do a bit of quizzing before we finally know what it all means.
To extend credit to farm syndicates and to provide a special account of some $25 million sounds very well. But as hon. members know, throughout the years this party has supported the economic family farm as the basis of Canadian agriculture, has supported the development of the co-operative ownership of machinery, has supported co-operative processing for farmers, has supported cooperative marketing, and has supported commodity marketing agreements between governments. In fact I think it is true to say that throughout the years this party has had some influence on agricultural policies in this house, closely associated as it is with the

producers of Canada, whether they are industrial or agricultural.
Until now we have not been faced with a bill quite like this one, but we have urged policies to this end and have urged legislation containing what appear to be the general purposes of this bill. We all know that in recent years, particularly since the second world war, there has been a great need for credit because of the greatly increased mechanization of our farms, and because of the large amounts of money required to buy the equipment necessary to service them.
I have had some experience of that in a much smaller field than on these wide prairie plains, or the rich Ontario valleys, or the rolling Quebec hills. It has been practical experience, because I am one of those who have their noses to the grindstone most of the time. Anyway this experience with the people I have the honour to represent has caused them willingly to associate themselves together in the co-operative purchasing of machinery, and I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) raise some doubts as to the ability of farmers to co-operate for this purpose. Our experience has been entirely different. We have carried on a form of co-operation in the purchase of machinery, as I said before on a much smaller scale than my hon. friends to the right speak of, but with great success, and I believe that what can be done in a limited sphere can be extended.
In his statement the minister recognized the great need for credit for the purchase of machinery, and also recognized the need for co-operative effort in purchasing machinery. Then he went on to deal with the syndicates, and this is the part of the bill on which we want full explanations. What does he mean by syndicates? How will they function? How will the proposed act be administered? I understand it is to be administered by the Farm Credit Corporation, and as this piece of legislation is an experiment its administration and application will be watched with interest.
As I have endeavoured to point out, there is experience in Canadian history to support this type of legislation in general principle. I am not quite sure of the details, but I remember when I was a boy our first investment in co-operative machinery was when all the neighbourhood got together to build a snowplow in order to get us out of the woods. Some people say we have not got out of them yet; but anyway, Mr. Speaker, after that we had co-operative ownership of

stump pulling machines. No one had sufficient money to buy a stump pulling machine and the necessary steam engine so we did it on a co-operative basis. Later we bought community land clearing equipment. Then as our orchards came into bearing we bought spraying machines on a co-operative basis, because these too were costly. In fact they are now ten times as costly as they were 40 years ago. Some farmers also went into the purchase of small saw mills and planers on a co-operative basis, and I shall have some questions to ask in that respect when we come to deal with various clauses in the bill.
Further, as has been pointed out, the prairies and other parts of the country shared similar experiences; all of which indicates that this type of legislation, if it is on a sound basis, should be very successful. Further we know that in the United Kingdom during the last eight or nine years they have experimented along these lines quite successfully. I do not know the details of their legislation with respect to co-operative ownership of machinery, but I do know the U.K. government makes provision for credit for the purchasing of machinery.
Because this is experimental legislation we have to ask a lot of questions. We support the principle or general purpose of the bill. Only experience in its application will determine whether it is successful to any extent or whether by amendment it can be made fully successful.
I take this point of view, Mr. Speaker. As I have said before, I give credit to the government for bringing in any legislation along this line that is of an experimental nature. We have to be willing to experiment in various ways in agriculture, as far as legislation is concerned. Some of these experiments will fail; some will succeed as the result of amendment because of experience. But I do believe we should be willing to see legislation of this type given a trial, to see how it works, and then look forward to an account from the minister, say after the act has had a year's operation.
I could go on at greater length, Mr. Speaker, but I think we can best get the information we require with respect to the purpose of this bill by asking our questions on the various clauses of the bill when they are being considered by the house in committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on the second reading of Bill C-121, an act to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates. We appreciate
Farm Machinery
the remarks the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture made last night, bringing to our attention some of the ramifications of this proposed legislation and answering some of the questions that have been asked. It is a refreshing change to have this Liberal government introducing for the first time since it was elected a piece of legislation that has to do with agriculture. Any other pieces of agriculture legislation, to the best of my knowledge, were concerned with amendments to existing legislation that had been introduced into this house by the Conservative party. It is unusual, Mr. Speaker, that when the government is introducing for the first time a piece of legislation concerning agriculture, the Minister of Agriculture is not present to pilot the bill through the house.
Mr. Speaker, may I make it abundantly clear at the beginning that I am in favour of any legislation that will help increase the farmer's income, or anything that can be done to reduce the farmer's operating costs. I would hope sincerely that this legislation would do just that, but I have very many doubts as to whether it will provide either of these two conditions. The first question I would ask the minister if he were here is: Why did he introduce this legislation? Did anybody make representation to him or the government asking for such legislation? Did the Canadian farm federation or the farmers' union make representation asking for this type of legislation? Or is this just a brainchild of the minister's, to help promote farm integration? Does he want to promote integration, or does he want to help the small, individual farmer? Or is this going to be just a great bonanza for the agricultural farm implement people?
I think there is a great deal of duplication in this piece of legislation. Farm improvement loans were extended just recently doubling the amount that any farmer may borrow. As hon. members know, this act was set up to enable farmers to buy machinery. I believe this act would take care of the very thing the government is trying to bring about in this bill. The Farm Credit Corporation legislation was recently amended and it, too, makes provision for the purchase of machinery.
Then we have the other lending facilities that are available. I think of the Canadian banking system and the banks that are ready and willing to extend credit to an economic farm unit or a farm operation that is on sound footing. I believe we should pause here for a moment Mr. Speaker, and think of

Farm Machinery
the part the bank managers and the banks of Canada have played down through the years in helping to develop the economy of our country and agriculture as well. I think of the very useful advice the bank manager can give to a farmer or to anyone who makes application for a loan. I do not think we can just pass by lightly the ability that he has and the information he has at his disposal; the guiding hand and direction he is able to give anyone making application for or inquiring about a loan. I say again that I believe there is a great deal of duplication in this piece of legislation.
Are these syndicates to be treated as a cooperative? Are they to have the advantages with regard to income tax returns that cooperatives have at the present time? If this is so, I think this is a discriminatory piece of legislation; I think it is unfair to private business. The man who has made a great investment in machinery, who is ready and willing and is doing business in his community as a custom operator, is being discriminated against by this piece of legislation; or will be if it is adopted by the house. I think of the many millers who are operating feed mills in my area and many other areas of Canada. It is suggested that mobile feed mills can be bought under a syndicate arrangement. These mobile feed mills will move around an area in which there is already located a mill that has been serving the area down through the years and has been rendering good service. They will have a distinct advantage over the miller in the community especially with regard to the income tax arrangements that will be provided to these syndicates under this piece of legislation.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think this will create unfair competition. I would suggest that if the minister wishes to aid the livestock feeder in the east or the west, a more direct approach might be taken. In my humble opinion, the present course of action that is proposed will give the greatest benefit to the machinery manufacturers. The progressive farmer has more to do than learn the complex workings of the feed trade. The organizing, operating, upkeep and financing of a mobile feed mill is no small problem. The knowledge required to use the mill to maximum efficiency, the knowledge required to mix uniform feeds for effective purposes, and the knowledge required to choose the right supplements to complement the farmer's grains are not learned overnight.

What happens then? Either there is the drop in quality that goes with a drop in price or some member, the one who has learned the most, will take over as manager of the group. If that is the case, the new co-operative group will be in direct competition with the local feed mill. It will incur many of the overhead costs which must be borne by any business organization and there will be fewer farmers to help bear these costs. A duplication of services often dilutes the efficiency of both.
I think this is a most unusual bill. There is a certain amount of mystery and experimentation connected with it. What research did the department carry out before introducing it? The parliamentary secretary told us last night that this system had been used in the United Kingdom. I believe he said it was introduced there in 1955 but that it took seven years, until 1962, to get 293 syndicates interested in this type of legislation. Even nine years later, in 1964, there were only 596 syndicates established under the United Kingdom program. Looking up the number of farmers in the United Kingdom I found that as of last year there were 399,683, almost as many as we have in Canada. However, I do not think a comparison can fairly be made between the situation in the United Kingdom and that which exists in Canada in this respect. The type of farming carried on in the United Kingdom is entirely different. They have smaller units there and climatic conditions are different from ours. So I do not think it is fair to say that because this scheme has worked in the United Kingdom it will necessarily work in Canada.
In conclusion I repeat what I said at the beginning of my remarks. I am in favour of anything which would help increase farm income or reduce operating costs, but I do not believe this bill is an answer to these problems. The measure involves duplication and for this reason it is not necessary. It discriminates against private businesses which are in operation in some fields one of which I have mentioned. For these reasons and others already mentioned, I doubt very much the value of this piece of legislation. I mentioned that this is the first piece of farm legislation which the Liberal government has introduced since it came to power and I cannot help think that they could have introduced much more needed legislation than is represented by the illconceived measure which has been placed before us at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to add anything to the arguments that have been advanced by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) (Mr. Danforth) and the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales), but I do feel that some observation should be made regarding the policy of this government to act on behalf of farmers and bring about within our country new hope in various areas of agriculture that have been so seriously neglected by this government.
In so far as this legislation is concerned, I can only measure its importance in the view of the government by the fact that no minister is here to present this legislation. Only two ministers are in the house. One is the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught), who at no time in my experience has participated in agricultural

Farm Machinery
matters, and the other, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet), whose experience in connection with agriculture is, to say the least, limited. I am not talking about his past, because I do not know anything about that, but I do know that his knowledge of agriculture has never been very apparent in this house. I am not going further than that at the moment, unless the hon. gentleman wants to get me into another field.
May I say this, and I speak with the authority of parliament throughout the years, that there could be nothing more contemptuous of the House of Commons than the introduction of legislation, which we are told is important, when the carriage of that legislation is not in the hands of a minister. I say that with all due respect to the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Beer), the parliamentary secretary. He cannot speak for the government and has no authority to do so. The answers he may give would not have the authority of governmental answers. Indeed I think this is the first time in the years I have been here that I have known of any legislation being inr-troduced without a minister being available to explain and answer the questions that necessarily arise.
When one thinks of the promises made only 17 months ago, 18 months ago and 19 months ago in respect of what was going to be done for Canadian agriculture, he must remember that now in the month of September this is the first matter of legislation originating with this government intended to help the farmer. Nothing has been done to meet the problem of the Canadian farmer, and that problem today relates to the increase in the cost-price squeeze and the increase in the prices of those things which the farmer has to buy without a corresponding increase in the price of those things the farmer has to sell. The government that promised much now brings in a piece of legislation that has all the appearance of papering over the agricultural cracks in the Canadian economy.
I was interested to read recently that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) thinks that the name "farmer" is one that is not as highly regarded as it should be. Indeed he said in his speech in Toronto on December 4 that something should be done to improve the image of the farmer, and that image he said should be improved in the sophisticated city minds. In the view of the Minister of Agriculture "farmer" is an expression that can no longer be used among the sophisticated, and therefore the Minister of Agriculture for Canada has concluded that it might be well to

change the name, and instead of calling him a farmer we should begin to call him what he really is, a food producer, a food manufacturer, or a grocery grower. That is a most unusual viewpoint on the part of the Minister of Agriculture for Canada, and it is surprising that he should be disturbed in his soul about the name "farmer" but not equally disturbed by the need for taking effective action.
Hon. members of the official opposition have brought before the house and the country the serious plight of the dairy farmers, the serious plight of the farmers both in Ontario and in Quebec. No action has been taken and nothing has been done to meet the problem, of such a nature in the province of Quebec that some
16,000	farmers-if I may still use that expression without its having the connotation of opprobrium that was in the mind of the Minister of Agriculture when he spoke in Toronto-marched on Quebec city. Nothing has been done and no action has been taken. The real income of the Canadian farmer is down, and I mean the effective income based on a proper relationship to the cost of things the farmer has to buy. Indeed what is being produced here by this legislation is simply an experiment with a potential $25 million cost tag attached to it.
I cannot discuss at this moment what the effect of this legislation will be, but it does provide that not less than three individuals, who are engaged in farming independently of one another, or who are members of a cooperative farm association, and the principal occupation of a majority of whom is farming, may obtain some assistance. What does this mean? It means simply that two farmers can join with a financially powerful man and then obtain this assistance. It is all very well to say that something should be done for the small farmer, and I believe in that, but this legislation has all the appearance of being ill digested, ill considered and completely insufficient in any way to meet the farm problems.
I am reminded that many promises were made by the Liberal party during the election campaign. They were summed up recently in the Family Herald of Montreal. I am glad to see that the joint minister of agriculture, if I may call him that, is in our midst now because he is the one who should be piloting this measure. He is the only one who can speak with authority, not a parliamentary secretary however estimable but a minister of the crown. I hope that as I go on the number of ministers will increase. I am referring to numbers, not to importance. We

now have three present and we will expect the hon. gentleman who has just come in, the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), to have something to say in this regard because, after all, in his own province of Quebec public opinion is aroused today to such an extent that one of the ministers said the other day the economic situation in that province was of greater importance than any constitutional matter that is being raised there.
I do not know why the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) felt that the word "farmer" carried a very unelevated connotation and whether that is the reason the present government has not acted to carry out its promises. They were wonderful promises that were made. Here they are as set out in the Family Herald:
The emphasis in price supports will be shifted from butter to skim milk powder and cheese. Deficiency payments will be made to cream shippers to maintain present price levels.
What has been done in that connection has left the dairy industry of eastern Canada -and I am now speaking of eastern Canada- in a most serious situation. Next:
A new Liberal government will take the initiative in formulating with the provinces a program of providing free milk for children in school.
Free milk? That promise, made in every part of this country, is gone. Next:
A new program of active leadership in improving the quality of dairy products will be undertaken in co-operation with the provinces.
Except for the change in the subsidy on Cheddar cheese there has been no action. Next:
Farmers who wish to switch from dairying to other enterprises to which their farms are better suited will be encouraged by credit specifically adapted to this purpose and by conversion compensation grants.
There is another program promised but no new measure has been produced.
Vigorous leadership will be provided in the activities in a new national co-ordinating advisory board for the dairy industry.
Promises were made and while a special dairy conference was convened the only board that is in existence is the national co-ordinating advisory board established by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) when he was minister. Then we come to wheat.
A new Liberal government will immediately provide a floor price of $2 per bushel for wheat-
Promise? Yes. Implementation? None. It has now been dropped.
Further, legislation will be provided for a two price system for wheat on the basis of the unit
Farm Machinery
quota. Farmers will be paid a price for wheat used in domestic human consumption which reflects the fact that they buy production requirements in a tariff protected market and sell in world markets. This policy will be effected by a consumer subsidy and thus will cause no rise in the price of bread.
No action. Forgotten. I mention these promises to indicate that what is being done here is simply a subterfuge to conceal the failure of the government to act on behalf of agriculture. What did they promise with regard to price supports?
A new Liberal government will maintain price supports on important agricultural products that are fair and realistic, they will be based on principles, not on expediency. Where appropriate, a new Liberal government will provide deficiency payments that will protect farmers in seasons of price declines by calculating payments on a quarterly instead of annual basis. Where appropriate, also, support prices will be put on a regional basis.
I need not tell you that that promise has been honoured by being entirely neglected except for the price support program on dairy products and the 47 cent support price on a pound of flue cured tobacco. Then we come to livestock improvement. To read this is like reading a book of fiction when compared with the implementation contained in this measure, which represents all that has been done except for the extension of credit under legislation already existing. This is what it says:
To further improve this vital section of our agricultural economy a new Liberal government will:
Rapidly expand record of performance testing of livestock...
Undertake additional aggressive programs of quality improvement for hogs, beef cattle, poultry and sheep.
Vigorously support research on livestock nutrition with a view to achieving significant cost reductions for farmers...
Undertake a thorough revision of the health of animals regulations and ensure their effective enforcement.
Nothing has been done on that last one. You will recall it was said that too much was being done for the west under the government of which I had the honour to be prime minister. All we did was to elevate the level in western Canada to that in other parts of Canada on behalf of agriculture. I speak now, not as Leader of the Opposition but as a western member wanting to see something done by the government on behalf of the eastern dairy farmers. Let us have no more of this tinkering, for that is what it is. The government will go out and say that they made $25 million available to syndicates. What the farmers are asking for is a fair and reasonable price level. Do you remember

Farm Machinery
what those on the other side of the house said? "We are going to bring about a new system. It has been most unfair for all ministers of agriculture to come from western Canada. We are going to give you an associate minister."
A new Liberal government will include both a minister of agriculture and an associate minister of agriculture of cabinet rank, one of whom will be specifically responsible for agricultural problems in eastern Canada.
A government of promises. A government of retreat. On the very first day as prime minister, the Prime Minister indicated it was his intention to appoint Mr. Rene Tremblay as the new minister of agriculture, east. That hon. gentleman thought he was appointed. He even had letterheads prepared and then he found there was not going to be one. That is the position of affairs today. This was a major promise and certainly with the Minister of Agriculture perambulating all over the country there should be a minister of agriculture present in the House of Commons to substitute for him and carry out some of these promises.

speechtext:
You could almost ask that question on all of these matters and develop a symphony in the house, a symphony in which all would say "nothing".
There is part of the record. 1 say that this government has totally failed to give consideration to the needs of Canadian agriculture. When the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) asked the other day regarding the turkey situation-and this was after the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) had spoken to those whom he called "the turkey people"-he was told that when the minister came back he would tell us about it. With the situation in our country, with the cost-price squeeze facing the Canadian farmer, the time has come for this government to wake up and bring in legislation that will be helpful. I repeat that western members and members from all parts of Canada will join with the government, if only it will act to meet immediately the one problem of transcendent importance to agriculture, the dairy problem in our country.
This legislation, the principle of which we accept and the performance of which we have little hope, does not even scratch the area of responsibility of this government in agriculture. It is nothing, as I see it, but a means of endeavouring to lead the people to believe that effective action is being taken. This legislation was promised months ago. I think about July 1 the minister announced that this legislation would be of great importance and that it would be brought in by about July 29. It is being introduced on September 22. No one knows where it was conceived. No one knows what agriculture organization has asked for it. No one knows how it will work. It is simply, as I said to begin with, a measure, grandiloquent in its terms, designed to cover up the fact that masses of promises respecting agriculture were made by members of the Liberal party,

Then they got the market in Russia, and yesterday we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) say everything is good in the country, and that there is a boom in progress. Certainly there has been a great improvement, so far as agriculture is concerned, since the Conservative party took office in the late 1950's, and that improvement is reflected today in the general economy of Canada, because when the wheat was sold it increased the gross national product of Canada and thus improved the general economic picture of the country.
During the 1962 and 1963 elections, when the Liberals were pouring out promises to win votes, we Conservative members told the people in our ridings, and elsewhere, that there was a bright economic picture, and that because the gross national product had increased by 6 or 8 per cent there was an uptrend in the economy. Did those farm champions, those cabinet ministers who are absent today, tell the electorate the truth at that time?
The Minister of Finance talked about the great Canadian, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the greatest living Canadian; but that same Canadian during the election told the farmers at Forest Lawn, in my constituency, that if his party were elected he would set a floor price for wheat at $2 a bushel. That was as much as he knew about agriculture. Hazen Argue had not been able to whisper to him that wheat at Fort William was then selling at $2.06 a bushel. The Prime Minister promised to reduce the price of wheat.
He also told the farmers that when the dollar was down valued they would get less for their produce and therefore would need more credit, but yesterday the Minister of Finance said that devaluing the dollar was the most important thing that led to the uptrend in the economy.
Now when the Liberals have found they have a market they are trying to take the credit for it. We have a travelling Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays). Someone said there was nothing wrong in having the parliamentary secretary steer this legislation

through the house, as the farmer says, "Somebody has to do the work. If I am going to sit in town the hired hand has to do the work," that is what is happening here.
As I said in my opening remarks, the law of supply and demand is important. If you have the demand, western Canada can supply it. As a man born and raised in western Canada I am convinced that if there were a food emergency in the world and the call went out, the western plains could produce not 600 million, not 700 million but a billion bushels of wheat, on present day farms with modern equipment.
The reflection of the economy of western Canada on eastern Canada is important. In dealing with credit for the purchase of farm machinery I want to refer to a speech I made on April 23, 1959. In it I gave the example of an average farm in the Bow River riding, and showed that the cost of machinery for it in 1947 was $37,000, while the same machinery cost $57,000 in 1959. In that short period the cost, of machinery increased by $20,000, and I shall try to be most fair about this. There has been an uptrend in the cost of machinery. We know that the kind of equipment used on farms has been much improved, and these improvements add to the cost of the machinery but, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, the farmer always faces the cost squeeze.
To people who may not be quite familiar with the economics of agriculture, when they drive into a farm and see a big combine, and see this and that, they think everything is fine on the homestead. But the cost of production is ever on the increase; and the government, as pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition, has done nothing to assist the farmer meet the cost squeeze. The only reason the farmers in western Canada are not in difficulty today is that the previous government laid the foundation for the markets for grain which brought prosperity and money to the farmers so they could purchase machines, pay their taxes and the costs of production.
But what has the government done today with regard to these markets? We read today in the farm papers and other papers that the Russian market has gone. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) is talking about exporting various kinds of new bulls from Canada; but they will not let them in because of the problem of foot and mouth disease. Has the minister really considered with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) the problem of new markets; because it will

take only one year in which to lose the markets that have been established, and the grain will pile up on the farms. The farmers really needed credit in 1956 and 1957, when they could not sell the grain. The previous government unloaded that surplus and laid the foundation for the markets which are now enjoyed by the Liberal government and have bailed them out of trouble, not only in western Canada but economically throughout Canada. That is the picture.
Let us analyse the bill itself. A typical farm today, in order to be an economic unit, must have at least a section, a section and a half or two sections of land in the wheat belts of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Today, with the type of farming that is undertaken, and nodoubt with the new kinds of grain scientists have brought out so as to shorten the period in which it will ripen, we are able to harvest the grain earlier. But we have that period in agriculture which we call the sensitivity period, the time when you have to do the work when the sun shines. I do not think this bill will be of any benefit to farmers who wish to purchase harvesting equipment, which is the most expensive type of equipment used on the farm. Last fall at this time I visited my own farm and drove one of those pusher combines which has just been made. It cost $12,000. This type of machine is necessary on the farm, for this reason. At that time the grain was swathed; it had been raining and the grain had started to sprout. When the time comes that the sun shines, you cannot have your neighbour using your combine, you have to be combining yourself -for two reasons; one is to get the grain, and the second is to keep the grade of the grain that is lying in the swath.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned, with regard to harvesting and seeding equipment, or general equipment on the farm in western Canada, this legislation is absolute nonsense. One of the closest friends of Harry Hays, the Minister of Agriculture, said it is absolute nonsense; it will do nothing. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, it is plain windowdressing. They are pretty thin drapes, at that; I am afraid everybody has seen through them. Do you know why this bill is brought in? It is brought in for the benefit of those who are going back to their constituencies, or those who wish to go into Conservative constituencies in western Canada, so they can say, "We at least did something for agriculture while Harry was absent". That is exactly what it is.

Mr. Speaker, just a word or two about Bill No. C-121, to tell the house that our party is in favour of the bill.
It does not commit the government but, above all, our farmers' credit. As for the government they will only have to take money out of the country's consolidated revenue fund.
Nowadays laws are constantly being passed to create new ways of getting into debt. Such is probably the new basis of our national economy.
Mr. Speaker, when this bill is being considered in committee I will probably have several questions to put to the Minister of Agriculture, but I very much fear that once again he will be conspicuous by his absence as he is this afternoon. I am obliged to make a few comments at this time so that they can at least be recorded if they cannot be answered right now.
We are all very much disappointed on account of the minister being absent when he should be in his seat in the house. If he is inadequately paid I would suggest that we increase his indemnity so that he would at least be present when the government is proposing amendments or legislation pertaining to agriculture and that he would show some interest in the agriculture of this country.
On reading this bill to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates, I am wondering whether this legisla-
tion will actually be useful in the province of Quebec.
Indeed, we find in the new Quebec farm programs a trend to extend each farmer's acreage. This need became evident when the farm loan legislation was discussed. Indeed, about 60 per cent of all loans were refused in my district because they said the farmers' acreage was too small. Today, our farmers are asked to have twice, or three, and even four times the area of their former land in order to be eligible for all those loans made available by the government.
Apart from those extended acreages, the smallest unit is 300 acres per farmer, we notice something else in the new policies and more particularly when there is forest farming. There are those community projects in Matane and Gaspe; I wonder when we are going to stop setting up community projects in order to come back to the family farm, which is so dear to our fellow citizens.
As I said a moment ago our farmers were asked to enlarge their acreage so as to be eligible for loans. And now that some farmers in my riding have bought four or five lots, which means about 500 acres, in order to negotiate a loan with a view to setting up a herd or buying mechanical equipment they are faced with another piece of legislation which in effect tells them: In future, we shall lend only to farm syndicates.
I know people who had to organize themselves on a family basis to acquire the minimum acreage required by the Farm Credit Corporation.
And, now that the head of the family has called upon his children in order to get enough land to entitle him to a farm loan, he is going to be asked to form a syndicate of at least three members. That means that, in future, three family units who have organized themselves these last few years will have to join together to try and benefit from those loans.
Frankly, I wonder if such a loan is not designed to favour some province other than Quebec. Not being familiar with the situation in the other provinces, I cannot tell whether they have enough of those machine syndicates to allow them to take advantage of the benefits provided for in Bill No. C-121, but I know the province of Quebec quite well and, at the present time, I am sure farmers there are not in a position to form those syndicates of at least three members to benefit immediately from those loans.
Considering the responsibility that will fall upon members of the syndicates as a con-

sequence of this bill, I wonder how that responsibility will be spread among the members.
Let us say that a syndicate has five, six or ten members, even though I doubt very much that such a thing will ever be possible in Quebec. Which of the ten members will carry more responsibility? Would it not have been better to provide in the bill for the issuance of an insurance policy to cover each member's share of the loan. If there were nine or ten members, a single policy would cover them all and on the death of the first one, the whole loan would be repaid. Indeed, I feel that other explanations will be necessary for us to form an opinion as to the responsibility of syndicate members.
For instance, the minister should state- because we will be asked that question in our ridings-who will be responsible, or if each farmer will be responsible, on a pro rata basis, for the amount he endorsed. I understood that they assume equal obligations, and since it is always the most solvent who is the most responsible, the whole thing is unfair and unpractical. I am asking my question in that light and, therefore, I claim that it will again be impossible for us in Quebec to get something out of that bill.
We are already having enough trouble with the loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation; we are having a lot of trouble getting it to accept a small number of the applications made by our farmers who need those loans.
Mr. Speaker, if the investigators called upon to deal with those loans are as strict as those of the Farm Credit Corporation, it should not be expected that this bill will be of any use in my area, because I follow closely the work of those officials and they are much more inclined to refuse loans than to try to help farmers to become eligible for them.
Over 40 per cent of farm owners in my area, that is, former farms that used to yield large crops, had to move to the city because their holdings were too small to meet the needs of their families. Those farms have remained uncultivated for five, 10, 15, and even 20 years. Those farmers are still waiting for government legislation, hoping that with farm credit loans, they will be able to return to those farms and cultivate them again. But, as the inspectors do not seem very much interested in putting those lands back under cultivation, farmers leave them and, sometimes on the advice of the investigators them-

selves, go to the city and try to sell their land to a finance or a trust company.
Mr. Speaker, I heartily wish that this bill will serve the purpose which the minister likely has in mind, but I think if he had glanced at Quebec, he would have soon realized that this bill would fall short of its objective. In fact, if he wanted to make it useful to Quebec, he would have to rewrite it almost entirely.
Why not pass a bill which would grant a loan to all farmers instead of those syndicates? Why not amend it to enable all farmers to take advantage of the measure? I think that it would be much more logical.
I heard someone from the western provinces talk about this bill and I concluded that if it had been introduced in the above-mentioned conditions, it would have been much more beneficial to farmers.
To conclude, I want to say that our farmers do not necessarily need loans, but concrete help. Under our present farming system, a loan is no help. Let us give our farmers what they ask for instead of what they did not ask for. They never asked for loans to purchase farm machinery. They need compensated discounts or subsidies in order to reduce the cost of those machines. That is what our farmers need.
Instead of throwing away millions of dollars to seek to control a small nation in Cyprus, why not use some of those millions for our own people, our farmers, by granting them compensated discounts on farm machinery?
If the sale of farm machinery cannot be controlled, I think the government would nevertheless have a major part to play by conducting inquiries on the cost of that machinery, and I am convinced that it can save for our farmers, from 20 to 25 per cent on the selling price of that machinery, if it would set a limit on the income of those companies, as well as a maximum rate of interest.
In doing so, it would help the farmers and, consequently, the whole of the people. The first duty of a government is to impose limits upon those who are tempted to go beyond them.
Even today, we hear that loans are granted at 30, 35 and even 40 per cent interest, and the government does not dare interfere with these loan sharks. I am wondering what useful purpose does the government serve? If there is one thing against which the farmers and all the Canadian people should be protected it is excessive interest rates.

This does not make sense; and when we ask the government to fix interest rates, to set a limit, it does absolutely nothing.
If a manufacturer or a seller is entitled to make 20, 25 or 30 per cent profit on the sale of an item, it rests with the government to fix a profit margin. But such a suggestion is made to no avail.
The government merely introduces measures such as the one which has just been passed to enable the farmer to get into debt, that is to authorize finance companies to take a tighter hold on him without any government control.
Instead of providing credit facilities for farmers, his cost price should be assured and more particularly, the marketing of his products should be guaranteed. The farmer would not need any loan then because he is no shirker.
Let us facilitate for him the purchase of farm implements at a reasonable cost, instead of forcing him to reimburse two or three times the cost. Let us secure markets for him and it will not be necessary to press him to support his family and develop our farm economy.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words in respect of this particular bill, and I shall be brief because I think most of the salient points have been covered by other hon. members. It would be a mistake on my part not to mention the effect of this legislation on the wheat farmers in my riding of Macleod, Alberta, and I limit my remarks to those individuals so there will be no misunderstanding about whom I have in mind.
If more than 1 per cent of all the wheat farmers in my area take advantage of, or benefit by the provisions of this legislation, that would be more than I would expect. This legislation is being advanced by the present government in an attempt to solve the problems with which farmers are faced today, and if less than 1 per cent of wheat farmers benefit, I suggest it will have little or no effect on the farming community of western Canada.
It may well be that several farmers in remote areas will get together and purchase a saw, for example, on a co-operative basis. I understand certain co-operative organizations in Saskatchewan have been purchasing machinery, and they might take advantage of the provisions of this legislation. We have yet to hear the minister clarify the effect of
TMr. Gauthier.]
these provisions on the Hutterite farming communities. I am sure we all want that information, so that we can in turn assess the effect the provisions of this legislation will have on different segments of the agricultural economy in this country. I am sure many others across Canada will be seeking information of this kind.
This legislation provides that those individuals who enter into a syndicate for the purposes of obtaining the assistance provided by this legislation will be jointly and severally responsible. In other words, if a man becomes part of a syndicate which obtains assistance through this legislation for the purchase of machinery, he becomes jointly and severally responsible in respect of that obligation. If I have any understanding of farmers and their philosophy, and I think I have, I know that they will not become involved in such a situation. Farmers are not inclined to sign on the dotted line and become responsible for a debt incurred by a syndicate, because they will not risk losing their land. I am sure that most farmers in western Canada who farm on a quarter section, a half section or perhaps even three quarters of a section will hesitate before forming a syndicate and becoming liable for the repayment of $100,000, for example, obtained through the provisions of this legislation for the purchase of new machinery. It is my experience that the farmers in western Canada usually buy second hand machinery which they can repair and use to harvest their crops, but which they can afford to purchase out of their available funds without having to risk having their land and assets attached. Farmers generally are wary of joining syndicates, corporations and organizations of that kind because they know they might lose their shirts.
I might also add that if five farmers formed a syndicate one might prefer to buy a combine, another might prefer to buy a manure spreader and another might want to buy a tractor; but if each one bought a particular machine they could exchange work and in this way get their farm work done rather than setting out to buy farm machinery jointly. In other words, the individualistic approach of the western farmer is going to have a great deal of influence on his thinking so far as joining a syndicate is concerned.
As for supporting the legislation, it provides for loans and may help co-operatives and others. Therefore I certainly will support it. However, the government is barking up the wrong tree if it thinks that this legislation is the solution of the farm problem of western

Canada. This legislation has to do with the provision of credit, and you do not look to credit for the solution of the problem of the farmers of western Canada. Their problem involves prices and markets. We were even told by the second speaker on the bill, a member of the N.D.P., that Liberal members from rural ridings did not support the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) with regard to this legislation. I have not had time to look into that statement but if it is true, and I believe it is, I wonder what those Liberal members would wish to support.
With all due respect, what we want to protect and perpetuate in this country is the family-size farm. It is the price which the farmer is going to receive for his wheat, his turkeys and other agricultural commodities which will determine whether he can keep his head above water and cope with the situation. The answer is not to give him more credit. If the government could do something to bring down the price of machinery they would be doing something that farmers and everybody else would like to see done, but there is nothing in this legislation that will bring down the price of machinery.
What the government is doing is to lend the farmers more money so they can buy more machinery, but this is no solution at all to the farm problem. Since I am talking to practically empty benches on the Liberal side, which indicates what they think about their agricultural program and the bill now before the house, I do not see that anyone else should be too much concerned. As I have said before, I intend to support the legislation and I hope it will do some good.

various agricultural areas of the country, where farmers could rent the necessary pieces of machinery from the department at the lowest possible rental charges. I can see that this is a very involved proposition. I believe that the measure now introduced by the Minister of Agriculture will overcome or at least contribute to overcoming one of the very great difficulties facing our farmers, the increasing high cost of machinery, which has tripled in the years since the end of the war. The parliamentary secretary indicated last night that machinery is now costing our farmers $541 million a year.

I am most disappointed at the typically critical, non-constructive and sometimes cynical attitude toward this legislation of some members opposite. I confine that comment to members of the official opposition who have complained bitterly about the inadequacies of the bill and about farm problems in general, but have put forward no constructive suggestions as to what might be done, first to improve the legislation, and second to improve the farm situation generally. We are well aware that there is a serious situation on the farms, particularly in eastern Canada. We know what the basic problem is. I think the leader of the New Democratic party summarized it very well in a speech last week when he dealt with the rising costs of operating a farm, and the decrease in the returns to the farmer from his labours and from the sale of his products. Other hon. members have already referred to this situation today as the cost-price squeeze.
This is the problem, but what is to be done about it? It is very easy to point to the problem and I am very concerned about it, as are all hon. members on this side. I have listened intently throughout this and previous

Farm Machinery
debates for one constructive suggestion from the opposition as to what might be done, and I have failed to hear one. While it is easy to criticize it is much more difficult to offer constructive suggestions and put forward ideas that can be enacted into legislation for the benefit of farmers in all parts of Canada.
I am also disappointed and somewhat disturbed by the attitude of members of the official opposition in indicating very strongly, it seemed to me, that our farmers are a group of people who cannot co-operate or work together. I deny that most emphatically. I was raised on a farm and have seen farmers work together. I cannot think of any occupational group of people who work together as well as farmers do, who share their machinery, plant their crops and harvest together. In fact, not only with regard to their agricultural problems but in their other pursuits and indeed, in every phase of life they work closely together, and I am most disappointed that members of the opposition would suggest, as they have almost invariably in speaking to the bill, that our farmers are a group of people who absolutely cannot take advantage of this legislation for the simple reason that they are selfish individuals who cannot work co-operatively for their own benefit, for the welfare of their industry and the common good of all farmers.
I am not going to enter into a discussion with the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) or some of the other members who spoke on all phases of agriculture, particularly in eastern Canada. The Leader of the Opposition had a very good opportunity yesterday to test the confidence of parliament in the matter of eastern agriculture or agriculture in general, but he passed up that opportunity. The other point which has been raised consistently by speakers from the opposite side has been the suggestion that this legislation will help only the large farmers. They seem to be gravely concerned that this government, and the minister, is interested in helping only the large farmer. Possibly they represent the large farmers, but in my part of the country we have many small farmers, and I think this is the situation in much of eastern Canada. I feel this legislation will do the exact opposite of what they have suggested, and that it will be of real benefit to the small farmer. The large farmer does not

have to depend on it; he has personal resources from which he can buy the type of machinery he needs most. The small farmer is not in such a favourable position. He must depend upon sources of credit such as are provided by this legislation in order to enable him to work in co-operation with his fellow farmers and purchase the type of machinery he requires. I think this is a very good piece of legislation-not perfect of course, but it is something new, something revolutionary, something farsighted, which members opposite can never see. It is something which will eventually, perhaps with improvement as may become necessary, benefit the small farmers of this country.
It has been suggested, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada are not concerned about additional credit. I should like to refer for a moment to a brief which was submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister of Canada and the members of the cabinet on February 26. On the matter of farm credit, the federation stated, in part, as follows:
The federation, at the federal-provincial agricultural conference in December of last year, made a number of submissions on farm credit to the government, urging in general much more intensive attention to farm credit needs, and the development of new programs. We will not repeat those representations here in full. In resolutions from our members, however, delegates to our annual meeting laid special emphasis on three immediate needs, which we would draw to your attention for early action:
First, they reiterated our long standing request for special disaster loan legislation.
I need not tell hon. gentlemen that this is the very type of legislation which we have introduced, and which is already in the resolution stage. I refer to the crop reinsurance measure. This will provide one of the requests of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
Their second request was as follows:
Second, the loan limit of the Farm Credit Corporation should be raised to $50,000.
We were even more generous than the Canadian Federation of Agriculture thought we should be. We raised it to $55,000. I continue to quote:
Third, the loan limit on farm machinery under the Farm Improvement Loans Act should be raised to $10,000-
Again, we were more generous than requested. We have raised the limit to $15,000.
Finally the federation said:
May we repeat that we feel well developed, flexible credit services to meet farm needs are

of utmost importance and deserve more intensive investigation and research than they have received in the past.
I think this measure answers very thoroughly the concern of Canadian farm people in having better sources of capital available to finance their varied farm activities, particularly in relation to one of the most difficult aspects of agriculture farmers have faced in recent years, the high cost of farm machinery.
I believe I have concluded what I wanted to say in this connection. I do not believe anyone would suggest this is a perfect piece of legislation. It is something new and something which I believe may be improved as experience dictates from time to time. There are two things which, from a personal point of view, I should like to see changed. I would prefer to see a fixed interest rate rather than a flexible one, which varies according to the cost of money at any particular time. I should like to see the service charge of 1 per cent eliminated. I feel that as a country we are not doing as much for agriculture as other countries are doing, and I think particularly of the United States, Great Britain and many European countries. The amount of money we contribute as a percentage of our budget or as a percentage of our total agricultural production, certainly is not comparable to the amount provided in other countries. I think the government should absorb the cost of servicing these loans and we should establish a fixed interest rate.
I mentioned that my original conception of this legislation was somewhat different from the measure the minister has introduced. I want to state emphatically that we on this side unanimously support this particular piece of legislation. We strongly support the minister. We have discussed it. We have advocated it and we feel it is a measure that will benefit farmers in all parts of Canada. If the farmers in some parts of Canada are too prosperous to take advantage of it, I can assure the house there are many farmers in eastern Canada who will be very happy to take advantage of it and I feel they will benefit immeasurably from it.

He asked certain questions and I will be only too glad to try to answer them. I should like to draw my answers from a document with which I am sure he is familiar. The caption is "A
Farm Machinery
square deal for farmers". This is a pamphlet put out by the Liberal party in 1962, wherein they said they had all the answers.
This pamphlet sets forth the basic problem. It is stated that the basic farm problem is the cost-price squeeze on the farmer's income. This is an important thing to remember when we are considering this bill, which is to provide credit for the purchase of farm machinery by syndicates. The other point that should be raised at this time, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that this bill provides for setting aside $25 million for the purposes embodied in the bill. I should like to refer hon. members opposite to the fact that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for this fiscal year amount to only $140 million. This measure apparently is so important it will require $25 million of the funds of this country in order to achieve the purposes for which this measure is designed and which, in my opinion, will affect less than 1 per cent of the Canadian farmers.
Those who want to know what could be done now for the farmers by way of legislation should look at the promises embodied in this election leaflet that was put out by hon. members opposite. I am just going to mention a few of those promises. These are some of the pledges made by the government and which were never fulfilled. In fact, no indication has been given that the government wants to move along these particular lines. First of all, you may think of the accelerated depreciation on farm machinery that was promised. You may think of the consumer subsidy that was promised on wheat going into domestic consumption. I think too of those promises that were made with regard to the stabilization act. What happened to the egg producers on the prairies during the last few months? I think too of the crop insurance legislation to which the hon. member referred when he mentioned disasters. The legislation to compensate for disaster promised by the government has nothing to do with the crop insurance legislation already on the statute books, and we have had no indication from the government of any legislation over and above the crop insurance legislation already enacted.
I also think of the impetus that could be given to ARDA in the areas where it applies. Mention was made today of the dairy problem in eastern Canada, and there was another promise made with regard to unemployment insurance for farm workers. That promise has been denied by the ministry and indications are that nothing will be done in

Farm Machinery
that regard. I could go on through this long list of promises, and hardly one has been touched upon by the administration.
Rosthern constituency probably has more small farms in it than any other riding in Canada. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, this bill is one of the most useless pieces of legislation ever to come before parliament. I am opposed to the principle contained in the bill. I believe it is a dangerous piece of legislation and that its very terms are a denial of the things the minister himself stated on so many occasions during the past several months, when he said the primary aim of his department would be to try to meet the problem of the farm machinery cost-price squeeze.
This bill does not lower the price of farm machinery. When one considers that $25 million is being set aside by this measure, and when one thinks of all the other things that could be done for farm people, and for people in other walks of life, with that $25 million, there can be no other conclusion but that there should be much more important legislation to present than this bill. I am going to oppose it because I believe it is wrong and because I believe farm people will be unable to use its provisions to any great extent.
The hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) said we have got to do something. That is the thinking across the aisle. They know they have to do something because they have not done anything so far. No one can deny that the Minister of Agriculture promised the farmers he would do something about the high price of farm machinery, but this bill will not in any appreciable way overcome that problem.
I believe this measure will encourage those speculative influences in agriculture that are likely to accelerate the destruction of the family farm. I am sure the speculators in western Canada will be much more interested in this measure than will farm people. It is an unthinkable thing that we are going to channel $25 million into this type of operation, after all the other legislation we have tried to enact over the years to help the family farm.
While there may be some-and their numbers will be limited-who will be able to use this legislation, its over-all effect will be to the detriment of the agricultural industry and it will be a retrograde step so far as farmers from one end of Canada to the other are concerned. Some have said this is daring legislation: I say it is foolhardy legislation.
To think we were told during the so-called flag debate that we were holding up something that was of importance, and now to be pre-
[Mr. Nasserden.l
sented with this bill just reinforces the comments I made on the resolution stage when I said this was one of the weakest measures ever brought before parliament on behalf of the agricultural industry.
