The proposals would not prevent shares being registered in the name of a Canadian resident where a non-resident is the beneficial owner, but in such cases no one would be permitted to exercise the voting rights pertaining to the shares so held.
No one would be permitted to exercise the voting rights pertaining to shares held directly by a non-resident or held for him by nominees if the total of the shares so held together with the shares held by or for shareholders associated with the non-resident exceeds 10 per cent of the issued shares of the company.
In order to prevent the purpose of the legislation from being defeated by transfers of shares between the date the bill is introduced and the date the legislation comes into force, and at the same time to avoid interfering with existing voting rights, the legislation would establish midnight tonight as a significant point of time in three respects. First, it will be proposed that if the directors of a company allow the entry in the company's books of any transfer of outstanding shares or allotment of newly issued shares to a non-resident after today that would increase the number of shares held by nonresidents beyond 25 per cent of the total number of issued shares, no one will be permitted to exercise the voting rights pertaining to the shares so transferred or allotted so long as they continue to be held by or for a non-resident. In the case of a company that today has more than 25 per cent of its issued shares held by non-residents, this suspension of voting rights would apply only to transfers or allotments of shares that would increase the proportion of shares held by non-residents, but the voting rights pertaining to shares now held by non-residents would not be disturbed.
Second, the prohibition against the exercising of voting rights, applicable in the case of any holding of shares by or for a nonresident and associated shareholders that exceeds 10 per cent of the issued shares, would not apply to any such holdings that now exist. However, this exemption would cease if any such holding is increased after today.
Third, if more than 50 per cent of the shares of a company are, today, held by or for one non-resident, that company would be exempt from these limitations on the transfer of

shares and the exercise of voting rights so long as that condition continues to exist.
I wish to remove any uncertainty which might otherwise exist following the introduction of this bill as to what will be proposed in the bills to amend the bank acts to be introduced later, concerning non-resident ownership and control. Provisions relating to this matter similar to those set forth in clause 3 of the bill to be introduced tomorrow and already described by me in this statement will be included in the bills to amend the bank acts, and these would also be effective after today to the extent that I have indicated for insurance, trust and loan companies.
I also want to make it clear that the proposals relating to non-resident ownership and control will not affect the great majority of normal market transactions in the shares of the institutions concerned. If trading is for resident ownership, these transactions are not affected at all. Transfers of shares between non-residents also will not be affected unless the transfer would cause a non-resident together with associated shareholders to own more than 10 per cent of the total number of issued shares.

speechtext:
This statement by the Minister of Finance has, of course, very wide implications, first in the investment field with regard to the powers of investment of trust companies and also in the much more complicated area of the ownership of financial institutions such as life insurance companies, trust and loan companies and banks.
I recall back in 1957 the measures brought in by the minister of finance at that time to prevent through mutualization, the capture of Canadian life insurance companies by foreign companies, if they were subject to take-over attempts. However these measures never prevented the gradual buying-in of these institutions, and I think it is this practice that the minister is trying to curb at the present time. Subject to what we may have to say when we see the bill and have considered all its implications, I think we must commend the government generally on this attempt. This is very complicated legislation as we can see from the conditions which will apply as described on pages two and three of the statement. I think I will reserve my remarks on the complexities of the measure until we see the legislation, except to mention that it has some of the complexity of certain anterior legislation which was presented to us and which has not worked out so well.

As I see it, the measure proposed will certainly not bring back some of our major life insurance companies which have been taken over, companies where more than a 50 per cent interest is owned by foreign investors. I think the third paragraph on page three covers that situation; it will remain undisturbed.
There is one point I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members. Insurance companies are to be given additional powers to invest in real estate and they will also be able to invest in subsidiary fire and casualty insurance companies in Canada, as well as in subsidiary life insurance companies. I think this is right, because our companies, particularly our fire and casualty companies, have gradually been taken over one by one by foreign owned concerns who have possessed this power while our own people, who frankly could have done so, were prevented by law from so doing.
One cautionary note I would raise relates to investment in subsidiary real estate companies. If these are merely realty holding companies for the purchase of a company's own premises, then it is not so bad. But I would not like to see this provision used as a means of involvement in speculative estate companies, because if there is anything which will get the reserves of a financial concern into a real mess it's having them tied up in real estate. We need only go back to the early thirties to be reminded of the position of United States financial institutions in this regard.
I feel that any further comment at this time would be superfluous; we will await the introduction of the legislation before making any further comment. However it seems to me that generally this represents a move in the direction taken by the minister's immediate predecessor but one.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on Bill C-121 I must first of all point out that at the time this bill was in the resolution stage I had many fears in respect of what it might do for Canadian agriculture, and many fears as to what it would do to the family farm position in this country. At that time I was assured by the minister that all my questions and fears were without foundation and would be dispelled when the bill was brought forward. We now have the bill, and as far as I am concerned I still see cause for questions and fears in respect of this supposed syndicate legislation.
There is no question but that today's agricultural picture represents a very important part of Canada's economy, and that money and management are the keys to agricultural
Farm. Machinery
success. Perhaps 20 or 30 years ago hard labour and long hours might well have been written in the record as being the key words to success on a farm. Today money and management might be said to be the two key factors in promoting and ensuring success on the farm. But as legislators we must ask ourselves what type of agriculture we are promoting. What types of farms do we foresee in the future? Several different pictures could be painted, one not necessarily in contradiction of the other, but nevertheless different modes of agricultural life exist in the world today. We look at Canada where we have a free enterprise type of agriculture, a personalized type of management in the operation of farms throughout Canada, with every farmer working and managing his own farm, looking after his own machinery and achieving one of the highest degrees of productivity throughout the world.
From time to time people take tours of Canada to study our agriculture. Not very long ago the Russian minister of agriculture toured Canada in an effort to ascertain why we were so successful in this country while they were not. What type of agriculture do we have in this country? As I pointed out, we have personalized management, a personal concern for profits, a personal effort on the part of the owner to make sure that he makes a comfortable living and is able to sustain himself. What type of agriculture does Russia have? One might say it is collective, one might say it is managed, but one can also say it is a syndicated type of operation for the welfare of the state and not necessarily for the welfare of the individual.
How much different is that from what this legislation will promote? This legislation establishes syndicates which will benefit the managers, but will it necessarily benefit the workers? How different is what this type of legislation promotes from the type of agriculture carried on in Russia today? Farms in that country are managed by the state and under this definition they would be syndicates with the workers taking care of the machinery.
In an article in a rural paper in western Canada the minister of agriculture from the U.S.S.R. pointed out that they have difficulties in that country because farm machinery is not looked after and the operators do not care because they do not own it. He said that he thought there was a difference. The minister and those with him visited farms in Saskatchewan and Manitoba where there were tractors and other machinery 10 years

Farm Machinery
old and they wondered why they were in such good condition. The answer they were given was: "It is mine, I look after it". That is the key to the management of farms across Canada today. How will that be promoted and extended by this legislation?

I hope it will promote and maintain the farm managed by the farmer for the benefit of the farmer and his family.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I for one am not apprehensive of this legislation as long as the syndicate is composed of farmers who really are working the land. I have only one suggestion to make to the minister in connection with this legislation. I think serious thought should be given to having these loans insured against the death of one of the participants. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that we have another bill before us which purports to help the farmer. As so often happens in this free discussion group here, a previous speaker rises and steals a great deal of your thunder. I could not have said better than the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) the things which are very close to my heart in connection with farming problems.
If the house will bear with me for a few minutes, there are one or two matters I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. I think we must consider very carefully the principle behind this bill. What are we going to do to farming in general? It is only a few years ago that our main problem, apparently- I do not say that I agree with this entirely- was that we had already produced too many agricultural products and we were starving in the midst of plenty. At that time our main problem was to find markets. I think the main problem is still to find markets. If the main efforts of our government were spent on marketing our products and making sure that the hungry people of the world were fed, for

instance, and that our prices in the world market were such that credit arrangements, and so forth, meant we were able to sell our goods, I think most of the smaller problems such as financing the farm would disappear.
I say this because if the farmers all across Canada had a ready market for their products, many of our problems in agriculture would disappear. I think it is safe to say that we are the only country in the world with far more virgin soil to be developed than we have developed so far. We have not yet reached our potential in farm production on the land we have. If our main effort is going to be toward feeding the world-and I think that is what it should be-and if marketing is to be our main objective, I believe this government should carry on in the vein in which we carried on in the six years we held office. We concentrated on the marketing of our goods, and, behold, many of the problems in agriculture were reduced.
Looked at from the human point of view, I for one was raised on the farm. I have no apologies to make for that because I think farming is now and always has been the most noble of all human endeavours. The feeding of people in our own country and then feeding the hungry people of the world is a blessing to mankind. This is certainly the role Canada can play far and above any other country, and this is the effort we should be making in this regard.
We want to keep people on the farm. I think the principle of this bill is entirely wrong. As the hon. member for Acadia said, this bill stresses making available large funds to farmers. They are certainly large funds to a small farmer or to a group of small farmers, if they can borrow up to $100,000. I do not think it is the financing of the farm that is the bottleneck. This bill purports to aid farmers in obtaining farm machinery and, I presume, at something like reasonable prices. What in the world is the use of a bill that requires the forming of syndicates, that requires considerable expense in getting together in a legal group, with all sorts of guarantees? How in the world will this reduce the price of farm machinery?
I do not see how this could do anything except raise the price by at least 1 per cent. That is written into the bill. It will cost money to administer the scheme and the cost of administration will be borne by the farmers themselves. So if we agree that this bill sets out to help the small farmer -and I do not think it does-it would begin

by adding at least 1 per cent to the cost of machinery bought under its provisions.
It may be a little more efficient to have one large tractor working on five farms, but my experience is that this is not possible. If there is a need to purchase one large piece of machinery I can see the need for a syndicate. But five farmers do not need a syndicate in order to get five tractors. Each farmer will naturally look after his tractor much better if he owns it outright and does not have to haggle with four other men. Rightly or wrongly, the Canadian farmer is a very independent person indeed. If he did not love his freedom I do not think he would go out and spend all the years necessary to put a farm into proper shape. This takes many long years of work not only by the farmer himself but by his family, gratis, and when they have produced a family farm they do not want four other farmers to help them run it.
I believe this is a thinly disguised way of providing assistance to corporate farming; I think this is the purpose behind the legislation, which is nothing less than a sop to this creeping socialism which is so prevalent in our country today.
The independent farmers in my own district, and I am speaking principally of them, each own between a quarter section and a section of land. Each needs one tractor. What they are worried about is certainly not the borrowing of $100,000 for more machinery. What they are worried about is getting a reasonable return for what they produce. If they can market their goods at reasonable prices they do not mind paying a reasonable price for machinery. It would take great ingenuity, I know, under our free enterprise system to devise a bill which would bring about a reduction in the price of a small tractor to the family farmer. But this is what he wants and this is what I should like to see him get. The small family farmer is worried about other things and I suggest the minister should turn his attention to other assistance measures which are of far more value even than lowering the cost of farm machinery, among them a guaranteed income. I do not go so far as to say that the department is actually against the small farmer, but I do believe the effect of this legislation will mean that the small farm will become smaller and smaller and that the large farm will become ever larger.
Do we want this trend to continue? We have heard a great deal lately about western farmers being in such good shape that they do not require any further assistance. This 20220-527i
Farm Machinery
could be true of the large grain farmers because in the last two or three years they have found a market for their grain. But by far the major proportion of the farmers in northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are small farmers. They are unable to pay the excessively high prices required today for machinery. Labour is short. It is necessary now for a farmer to farm his own land and the argument that the large farm or corporation farm is more efficient is not a good enough answer for us in Canada.
As hon. members opposite well know, because it is their pigeon now, we face a folding up of many railway branch lines. One reason for this is that there are fewer people living on the land. It takes a courageous government to reverse this trend, a trend which I say is wrong. A corporate farm may be able to produce wheat at $1.20 a bushel whereas normally it would cost $1.40, but we will always require in Canada a strong, independent minded people who come from rural surroundings. I do not think there is a man in this house who if he were to look into his ancestry, would find himself more than three generations off the farm. When families move into the cities, they die out. I challenge anybody in this house to say he can look back for three generations and not find that his grandparents or great-grandparents came from the farm. This is a heritage we have to preserve, and that is why I ask the house to consider this whole matter very carefully. This new economic religion we are preaching today, this religion of efficiency, efficiency, efficiency, may have a serious effect on the future of our country.	1

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Athabasca a question? This afternoon in my speech on this subject I mentioned the percentage of farmers in my riding who I thought would be making use of this legislation. What is the view of the hon. member with respect to the constituency of Athabasca, where there are a large number of small farmers? Would it be 1 per cent, or would it be less?

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
I think 1 per cent would be a liberal estimate, if I may use that term. Certainly the suggestion contained in this legislation has never been put forward to me, and I have attended every farmers meeting in my district during the past six years. I have never attended a farmers meeting without this question being put to me-and I admit it is a difficult one to answer: How can we reduce the cost of farm machinery on the family farm? If the present bill purports

Farm Machinery
to do that, I think it is a colossal failure. I cannot see that by adding legal costs to the already extremely high cost of farm machinery we shall be doing a thing to help the farmers.
But we must do more than try to reduce the initial cost of farm machinery. I understand from the farmers in my area that they are greatly concerned at the present time at the cost of maintenance and repairs. I will give hon. members a concrete example. Only two years ago I was out in a harvest field with one of the farmers in my constituency. Some time earlier his combine had broken down. He had sent his son to town for the spare part required and his son eventually arrived with the piece of repair material. It was a chain. No doubt some members will recognize it when I describe it as an elevating chain for hoisting grain into the combine where it is threshed. The farmer showed it to me and said: "What do you think would be a fair price for that?" Well, it was two pieces of chain a little heavier than bicycle chain, about 20 feet long-two chains 20 feet long very similar to bicycle chain, built the same way. And there were crossed slats set about 15 inches apart, made of bent aluminum. I looked at it. I am not a machinist but it seemed to me that allowing for the automation they have in industry, facilities for turning out this kind of thing by mass production, $50 would be a fair price. Believe me I was giving what I thought was a liberal estimate of a fair price for that piece of machinery. Well, it cost that farmer $248. It was just five times the price I thought it should be. I have had some experience on the farm. I have also worked in a hardware store. Yet I could not see how this was worth more than $50 in any circumstances.
This is the kind of problem which alarms the small farmer. His turnover is not large and after he has paid $9,000 for a combine he is worried about the cost of keeping it in operation. What are we going to do about that? That is perhaps a difficult question to answer. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture and the officials of his department might call together the manufacturers of farm machines and ask them what they intend to dc. about lowering the cost of farm machinery and repairs.
This whole situation is not a one-way street. We are not shy about asking the farmer to put his shoulder to the wheel in time of war to produce more and more food and peg the prices of his products. Why can-

not the farm machinery manufacturers do something to reduce the cost of repairs?
I am not so cynical that I believe the Massey-Ferguson people are not interested in the welfare of this country and particularly the farmer. Well, they should be interested because if my figures are accurate their profit for this year exceeded the profit for any year in their history, and at a time when the farmers of this country are asking this government to do something about reducing the price of farm machinery. I think there should be a limit to the profits of the farm machinery manufacturer. What would people do if the farmers were to create a monopoly on food, holding it on the farms until they received an exorbitant price? I am sure every newspaper and member of parliament, particularly those representing urban ridings, would castigate the farmers of this country if they held their grain on the farm until they received $4, $5, $6 or $7 per bushel. The people of this country would become alarmed if that situation occurred.
The Minister of Agriculture should make some attempt, in co-operation with farm machinery manufacturing companies, to reduce the cost of farm machines and repairs to farm implements. The Liberals and Conservatives, being members of the two free enterprise supporting parties in this house, should get together with management in an attempt to find a solution to this price squeeze problem. Let us challenge the manufacturers to find a solution to this problem.
No one who has heard me speak in this house could think that I am a socialist. I am against socialism in all its creeping forms. I do not think that the Saskatchewan river dam project is a socialist project but rather an investment in which we should all share. I do not think subsidies paid in certain circumstances, particularly in respect of freight rates for the shipment of livestock, is representative of socialism, but some people would make that suggestion. However, I am opposed to this kind of legislation and suggest that it is a socialistic measure, because it in effect states that individual farmers can no longer own and operate their own farms and at the same time obtain assistance under the provisions of this bill. It suggests that farmers must form a corporation of three, five, seven or a million. The basic principle of strength in our economic national life has always been that one man may own and operate his own farm. I am against corporation farming in all its phases. I think it is very dangerous

to have more than half of the production of food in Canada being produced by corporations.
This bill states that the majority of people to be assisted under this farming legislation must be farmers. It is astounding that that fact must be spelled out in this legislation. I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture has spelled that out in this bill in an attempt to bring a halt to the trend toward the complete takeover by corporations of farming in Canada. I think we should take a very serious look at the situation. I do not think it is wise to turn our land over to corporations and allow them to produce all our food, including grains, poultry and cattle. Why must we spell out in a bill as this that the majority of individuals to benefit will be farmers, and then limit the assistance to groups or corporations? I do not wish to name the corporations, but the effect of this legislation will be that those groups will be able to obtain vast sums of money for the purchase of farm machinery with which to operate in direct competition with the small farmer of the type I represent, who on his own is unable to obtain the same assistance.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) suggested perhaps 1 per cent of the wheat farmers in western Canada would benefit as a result of this legislation. I do not believe that one quarter of 1 per cent of the wheat farmers in western Canada will benefit. I think the benefit of this legislation will be reaped by those corporations which are engaged, and are becoming engaged, in farming. As long as the government is assisting these corporations by guaranteeing prices and developing markets farming will be profitable on that basis.
I do not believe in nor will I support anything that tends to assist and encourage large groups or corporations to buy farms from the individual farmers who have worked all their lives to make a living. I would support any kind of legislation which would help make it possible for the boys and girls who have been raised on the small family farms in Canada to take over those farms from their parents and operate them as family farms, and I will not support any legislation of the kind that suggests men should gather together in groups or corporations in order to operate farms in Canada. People should be allowed to group together of their own volition, and I am thinking in terms of the Hutterite colonies which exist in Alberta. In many cases even they are being persecuted, but if they wish to gather together in that fashion it is their right to do so. I do not think people should be forced to
Farm Machinery
form corporations in order to take advantage of assistance offered by the government.
The Minister of Agriculture may well suggest that there is nothing in this legislation to compel farmers to form groups, but the only way they can take advantage of the provisions of this legislation is by doing exactly that. If a group of individuals wish to obtain $100,000 for the purchase of farm machinery they must form a group or corporation and assume liability jointly and severally.
Cheaper farm machinery cannot be obtained by hiring a lawyer to incorporate a group or by incurring the expenses of civil servants to inspect the farms to ascertain whether they are good risks. Let us do something about reducing the cost of farm machinery. Let us do something about reducing the cost of maintaining that machinery. Once we do that thousands of individual farmers across this country will believe that we are assisting them.
The only excuse I can find for the minister in respect of this legislation is that he does not fully understand the effect of it. If he does fully understand the effect of the provisions in this bill and realizes that it is a form of socialism, supported by those members to my left, then this legislation is worse than it appears on the surface.

I sincerely hope that they will not, and that is one of the reasons I am taking part in this debate. I do not think my words fall entirely on deaf ears. If I can show hon. members that this legislation is not in the interests of the average small farmer in Canada I am sure some hon.

Farm Machinery
members, even in your party, will be broadminded enough to oppose it.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry if I have offended the hon. member by my castigation of socialism, but when considering the end result of this proposed legislation one must realize that it is a form of socialism. I commenced my remarks along that particular line.
The principles of this bill should be thoroughly understood before we are called upon to make a decision. If there is any provision in this bill which in the end result will be of assistance to the family farm I will support it, but I do not believe that to be the case. If there is anything in this bill which will promote the welfare of the individual farmer in this country I will support it, but I think we must look at the end result of its provisions before coming to a final conclusion. I do not think any provision of this bill will promote that welfare, but will in fact do quite the contrary-increase the cost of farm machinery. I think this legislation is a smokescreen behind which the ministers can hide. We are being asked by this legislation in effect to sign several blank cheques. I do not think we fully appreciate exactly what this bill will accomplish.

speechtext: Order. May I bring to the attention of the hon. member that on second reading we are limited to a study and consideration of the principles of a bill, and the hon. member cannot discuss a study or consideration of individual clauses.

speechtext:
I have been trying to establish the principle of the bill as well as I can. I think any hasty legislation loses sight of the principle, and it is the principle of the bill which I am attacking, I hope with some approbation in the house. I am sure that anybody who believes in free enterprise will say that the emphasis should be upon individual, free enterprise and that people should not be forced into corporations. Perhaps in other industries some people have been forced into incorporating, but I think most of us will agree that generally this is done to escape taxation. When an individual starts making excess profits, shall we say, he immediately turns to his lawyers and has them form a corporation so that his excess profits are still retained within a very narrow group.
I suggest that the same type of thing will go on under this legislation in that excess profits might be made from fattening livestock, let us say, by people who are not really farmers at all, and they are going to hide these profits by spreading them five ways.

Only two of them may be farmers and another may well be a millionaire who has no connection whatsoever with agriculture. It is this principle I am attacking, and I am quite sure that I am expressing the opinion of a great majority of the members of my own party, although I do not pretend to speak for the Conservative party as a whole. On this side of the house we do not do that. We speak at all times according to our consciences and on the basis of what we know. We are not a group of experts in any respect. I have never owned a farm, although in my youth I worked for several years on farms for very little remuneration.
I am not an expert on farming but I have taken the trouble to talk to people who are, to people who have hacked their own farms out of the bush and now live in the hope that by working hard and long and doing their best they can earn a fair and decent living. When I visit these farmers it is the cost-price squeeze I am always hearing about. They want to know why it is that no matter how high the prices for their products go the price of machinery always goes higher. This is why I suggested to the minister-I would be quite willing to go along with him if necessary- that he should talk to some of the people who produce farm machinery and discuss whether this is a good time to expect excessive profits. The farmer has often been asked if he would not work a little harder to produce cheaper food for the hungry people of the world, and it is a good question. Would the farm machinery people not be willing to give a little so far as their profits are concerned toward the same end? Certainly we could produce cheaper grain if we had cheaper machinery.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, it is also a mistake to assume that all the problems of agriculture in western Canada are solved. I might say that in the northern half of Alberta comprising the constituencies of Athabasca, Jasper-Edson and Peace River there are more individual farmers than there are in the other eight constituencies south of the North Saskatchewan river. This supports what I said, that if we are thinking about agriculture it is the small bush farms where we find the people who are replenishing the good red blood of our country. They are on farms and this legislation will not help them at all. It will only add unnecessary cost when what is required is the cutting down of the original cost of machinery and the cost of maintenance. This is what will help them most.

We must tie in this farm legislation with other farm legislation. There is certainly no point in providing this type of credit to the farmer unless you are going to be able to guarantee in some way that the help you are giving him with your left hand is not going to be taken away by your right hand. All these things must be integrated. Under ARDA the scientific use of our land is certainly a national project, but there is no point at all in taking people off submarginal land and putting them on good land unless they are going to retain the important things-the right to own their own land, the right to stand on their own feet.
I think it is a preposterous thing for us to go to the taxpayers of this country and ask them to subsidize any type of corporation. That is my own personal opinion. I do not believe in corporations being subsidized by other people at all. If five wealthy farmers are willing to pool their resources they do not need any help from the government at all. They can go to any bank in Canada and borrow money.
I want to make another point about the question of interest. The bill purports to assist farmers to obtain agricultural machinery at reasonable prices. What is the interest rate going to be? I am trying to keep away from the specifics of the bill, but because the interest rate is left blank the whole principle of the bill to my mind falls down unless we are going to be able to assist farmers to get machinery at a reasonable price and at a reasonable interest rate. Part of the principle of the bill is surely the interest rate. There is no point in lending money to farmers if the interest rate is going to be excessive. I would ask the minister to explain later exactly what interest rate he expects the farmers will have to pay.
When we were in office and introduced farm legislation our principle was that because the farmers were in fact the backbone of the country we should make money available to them over a long period of time at a reasonable interest rate, and so we established an interest rate at 5 per cent on farm loans. With any higher interest rate I do not see how the bill will be of any help at all, particularly to the small farmer.
When the minister travels throughout the country I should like him to make sure he does not add to the rift or arguments between the east and west. I would say that our problems in the northern part of Alberta are much more similar to the problems of the farmers of eastern Canada and the maritimes
Farm Machinery
and the small fruit farms of British Columbia and Ontario than to the problems of the large grain farmer. I am not saying at all that there are not problems in western Canada of pressing importance, but as long as we can maintain our world trade in wheat I think that the major problem of the prairies is temporarily resolved.
I say that the small farms of northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba are the same as the farms of eastern Canada and the maritimes and the problem we are faced with is how to make sure that these small farmers have a minimum income. I do not think it is any answer to say that if a man cannot make money on the farm he should pack up and go to a city. What are these people going to do in the cities? We are faced with automation and excess labour in the cities can no longer be absorbed. They can suceed on the farms and we have to arrive at a happy medium between so-called efficiency and maintaining happy people on the farms.
While it is a desperate step, one solution might be to institute some form of licensing in order to protect the family farm. We must be ready to define a farm. I see that in the bill it has been found necessary to define "farmer" for the purposes of the legislation. This might be a good time to take a look at defining who is a farmer and who is not, and in doing this we would have to get a very clear idea of what type of farmer we intend to assist-not to subsidize but to assist-by creating an atmosphere in which he can operate.
Some years ago the farmers from western Canada came down here and I faced them with this problem. I said, what is a family farmer? Some of the spokesmen for this group were shy about defining a family farmer. I do not know why they were afraid to do so, but I suggest perhaps even within the farmers union there are influential people who have a great stake in farming and who do not want the farmer too closely scrutinized. They do not want to say, this is a farmer and this is not. I am quite sure that when the time comes to administer this measure you are going to have a great deal of difficulty in deciding who is a farmer and who is not, and how much of his income is derived from farming.
I have never hesitated to define a family farmer. I say a family farmer is one who lives on the land. I for one am against subsidizing or assisting or encouraging anybody else through special legislation who is not

Farm Machinery
in fact a bona fide resident on a farm to go into agriculture. I do not believe Canada Packers are farmers. I do not believe the sugar people are farmers, but they are deeply entrenched in the farming business, as you know. This is where these corporations come into the picture. Suppose you are seized with the problem of deciding whether or not a machine for digging sugar beets should come under this legislation. What are you going to do there? Will the Rodgers Company or the Alberta Sugar Refiners be considered farmers? Will they be considered farmers merely because they take up a quarter of cleared land? This is vertical integration and it has gone away beyond bounds in Canada today. It is only a few years since, to my knowledge, one corporation in Ontario was producing 50 per cent of all the broilers. I pose this question for the Minister of Agriculture. This corporation is still in existence. Perhaps they will decide to grow grain for their own chickens, and if you get a few small farmers in southern Ontario with 50 acres and you include this corporation, which I will still leave anonymous, as the third party, are you going to lend them another $100,000 in order that they can buy some farm machinery to put another 30 or 40 farmers out of business?
Are we merely trying to cut down these large corporations and make them standard across the country? Are we going to say that you can no longer farm unless you have a financial corporation as a silent partner?

to impose their will on anybody. The only difference between socialism and communism is the amount of force required. Nevertheless I have not strayed very far because I have put up a warning light for my Liberal friends so they will not fall into this socialist trap. If the bill is intended to force us into communal farming, then it is socialism. It may well be communist in its final analysis, if that is the purpose of the bill. I object to it on these grounds. We Conservatives stand for the maintenance of the standards of our ancestors. We do not have to go too far back, two or three generations. Our ancestors pioneered this country and believed when they established themselves as farmers they would be able to hand on to their children a well established way of life.
They did not intend that at any time their representatives in parliament would sell out to socialism or to the larger corporations. It is not fair. Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-121 brings us to define the role of agriculture in society. It plays one of the greatest, noblest roles because the farmer needs several organizations; he has to work for several segments of the economy before he can reach his objective. The purpose of agriculture is to provide food for individ-

uals, for human beings. We must recognize and appreciate the true value of agriculture. Why is agriculture important? What is its role? What is the reason for its existence?
We absolutely have to admit, as members of parliament and as individuals, that agriculture is the cornerstone, the basis on which rests the whole structure of society.
However, if the foundations of agriculture are undermined as they are at present, then the whole economic and social structure of society will disintegrate. Because if it is recognized that farmers have basic needs, that agriculture, especially in the province of Quebec, is at present in a terrible state of stagnation, members of parliament and several public officials are still not aware of it. If members of the house visited rural counties in my part of the country, they would realize the chaotic state of agriculture in our districts and would see that 70 per cent of farmers have abandoned their farms.
It is real stagnation. Those remaining express the desire to leave the farm from day to day, from month to month. Since no help was provided to the farmers, today the family farm is gradually disintegrating and disappearing. It is the result of our present system, and this phenomenon of the disintegration of agriculture is also evident throughout the economic structure.
Farmers have vital needs. They need a home just as the city worker, as any other individual in the country; they need clothing, they would like to give an education to their children the same as anyone else. And with an average annual farm income of $1,500 in the province of Quebec, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) cannot believe that his Bill No. C-121 could be applied in that province. Does he think that the eastern farmer could take advantage of that legislation?
Everybody knows that 99 per cent of the farmers are already saddled with farm loans; they have a hard time making ends meet and discharging their obligations. The Duplessis government had granted farmers loans which, as he claimed at that time, were to save agriculture in the province of Quebec, get farmers out of the doldrums; but 20 or 25 years later, one finds that farmers are ten times worse off than they were before.
Farm loans proved that they were not the right formula to save agriculture because experience showed that they served only to get farmers into debt and into worse trouble. Farmers operated their farms during 10, 15 and 20 years without showing a deficit and now they wake up with one. Farmers obtain 20220-528
Farm Machinery
loans offered by the federal and provincial governments and those new loans only serve to pay off the deficits incurred in the last 10 or 15 years.
And the farmer is left with his run-down buildings and his broken agricultural instruments. In fact, there is hardly anything he can use any more. He is then obliged to borrow $15,000, $20,000 or even $25,000 to make up for his deficits in previous years.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot see how this measure can save agriculture. We are not opposed to the principle of the bill. But this measure only favours those who have money; it is of no help at all for those who have none. As a matter of fact 99 per cent of the farmers will not be able to take advantage of this piece of legislation because they are already so deeply in debt that the banks will probably refuse to let them have a loan even if the government does guarantee such loans. I do not see how this bill could solve the farm problem.
Yet, there are solutions to the farm problem. But proper action should be taken to solve existing problems if we really want to help the farmers. Anything else would be of no earthly use and would never solve the problem. Many suggestions have been made over the years, but none were accepted.
Agriculture is more than ever in a state of stagnation, and it is not by making loans to the farmer and by charging him interest that his problems will be solved. As a matter of fact, he cannot even make enough profit to pay the interest and if he has to pay interest on farm loans, it will increase the cost of production and, consequently, the cost of living will rise as is the case at the present time.
As a matter of fact, it seems that there is no end to it.
Are we going to solve the agricultural problem with all the methods that were suggested and the measures that were applied? I do not think so, as agriculture is still in a state of depression and nothing has been settled yet.
Therefore, in order to solve the agricultural problems, I will allow myself to make a few suggestions to the Minister of Agriculture as well as to the house. I know that several members have already made suggestions, but I suggest that since agriculture is in a state of stagnation and the farmer is unable to pay any interest, the money that will be lent him should be interest free. This is one of the first steps to be taken if the agricultural

Here is my second suggestion. It was pointed out a while ago that farmers needed homes and farm buildings, and yet taxes have been raised. As a matter of fact, farmers are building the year round. But an 11 per cent sales tax has been imposed on all building materials, with the result that the farmer has to suffer the ill-effects of a tax increase he cannot afford to pay. So let us start by removing taxes which are hurting everybody, but especially the farmer. Let the Minister of Agriculture begin by removing that tax. I would also suggest to the minister that all the heavy equipment the farmer needs to clear up and enlarge his farm and to help him do his work, especially when there are many stones on his land, ought to be made available to him and paid in full either by the provincial or the federal government or by both together, or through shared programs under ARDA.

subtopic: POULTRY
POULTRY
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO MAINTAIN PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I asked to have this question debated is because it is of such importance and urgency. On many occasions I have asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) about the low prices for turkeys, and he gave me the answer that they were higher than ever before. When I asked him about the low prices for livestock he gave me the same answer, that they were higher than they ever were, when in fact they were at their lowest.
The other day when I asked why the price for chickens was so low, Mr. Speaker said I should put the question on the order paper; but as I have already said, it is of such importance and urgency that I would like to debate it now.
I have here in my hand a sales slip issued to a farmer in my area, Mr. Olaf Olson, who sold 99 chickens. After they had deducted $9.50 for killing these birds, he finished up with $8.35 for them. Mr. Olson lives about 40 miles from Humboldt. If you consider the 10 cents per mile that is usually charged for travelling, it will be seen that he wound up with only 35 cents for the whole works. In order that hon. members do not get the impression that these chickens were of poor grade I would like to give the record that is to be found on this sales slip. There were 12 grade A's which weighed up to 5J pounds killed, 60 B's that weighed up to about 4J pounds, 17 C's, and there were two or three old roosters and chickens of lower grade. But the fact is that any time a farmer sells 99 chickens at grade A, B and C and only receives $8.35, there must be something wrong. It is for this reason that I bring this question to the attention of the house, because when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) goes out in the country and tells us that the price of livestock, poultry and turkeys is higher than ever before, the fact is that this is not the case.
The same thing applies to turkeys. The price of turkeys is lower than it has ever been before. The Minister of Agriculture has not done anything to solve this problem, and I suggested to my good friend Mr. Olaf Olson that what he should have done was take a hatchet, go into his chicken coop, chop the heads off the chickens, give his chickens a decent funeral and forget about the whole thing. He is a good Swede, and when I told him this he looked at me. He did not say

very much; he only swore, and I would not like to say exactly what he said.
I would like the Minister of Agriculture to give me and the people in the country an answer to his question. Why does the farmer only receive $8.35 for 99 chickens, when they are bought in the store for a much higher price?

Mr. Speaker, here is the question I should like to put to the minister and which will be answered, I am sure, by her parliamentary secretary, who is here now, with great ability and in a very appropriate manner.

I have already put this question in the house. The minister then replied, very properly indeed, that she was not in a position to give me a specific reply.
What happened is that because no precise decision has been taken in that respect, the said winter sports association of Quebec city finds itself in a difficult situation. In fact, under the present circumstances, it will have to postpone until 1967 the project it had intended to undertake in 1966.
Having received very recently a written as well as a verbal communication from the president of that association, I thought it was my duty to bring the matter up again so as to know what to expect, in order to be in a position to give a specific and final reply to the interested parties.
I would like to know if that subsidy will be granted according to the recommendation made.
If no grant is forthcoming, I should like to know why. Are there legal, political or constitutional difficulties in the way? That is what I should like to know in order to give an adequate reply to the people concerned who have asked me for information.
Nothing would please Quebec citizens more than to see that project carried out at the very centre of French life in America, so that during the celebration of our centennial, in 1967, all our athletes, united in a spirit of solidarity, will participate in competitions. That endeavour will be a great success if the federal government agrees to give the requested grants.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF RUSSIAN
APPOINTMENT OF RUSSIAN
subsubtopic: PROFESSOR AT UNIVERSITY OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sought leave to debate this matter this evening because I was denied the privilege of receiving an answer to my question to the minister this afternoon. He did not even choose to take my question as notice, which would have permitted him to give a brief and concise answer tomorrow.
My question arises from an announcement which appeared in the Leader-Post of September 18, 1964 under the heading "Russian to Teach". This article states:
A. B. Nicolaev, 41, an economist from Moscow State university has been appointed visiting professor of economics at the University of Saskatchewan, Regina, campus. Mr. Nicolaev is deputy chairman of the department of political economy at the university. He was a guest lecturer at both Cambridge and Oxford, 1962.
Principal W.A. Riddell said today he believed it was the first time a Soviet citizen has accepted a
[Mr. Choquette.l
post to a Canadian university. The invitation was extended with the approval of the external affairs department.
Further to that announcement a release was made to radio and television stations, and a comment was credited to Professor Smythe, who I understand is head of the economics department at the Regina campus, to the effect that this Russian economics professor would be of great benefit and would give intellectual stimulation to the student body.
It might well be that the minister and his parliamentary secretary will say that this is a provincial matter. I believe that questions will be asked of the provincial authorities, but as a member of this House of Commons I do not have the oportunity to do that.
As a result of this announcement made on September 18 I have received several letters from people who are aroused about this professor coming to Regina. Some of those letters were written by parents of students who wonder about the orientation in the university as a result of this visiting economics professor. I do not share in full those fears and concerns which have been expressed, because I am aware of visits being made back and forth between the U.S.S.R. and this country, and our exchange in trade, which is leading to a new understanding. The fact remains that people in communist countries have relatives who are naturalized Canadians. Immediately those Canadians apply to have those relatives released and allowed to come to Canada where they can find the freedom offered in this country, their requests are given short shrift. Yet with apparent alacrity this leading professor of economics from the University of Moscow is permitted to come on a visit to fill a fellowship position in the economics faculty of the University of Saskatchewan, Regina campus.
It is said that this has been done with the full approval of the federal government and the Department of External Affairs. Therefore at the federal level there are questions that I think should be completely answered so that the fears that people have with regard to the spreading of communism in a seductive manner will be allayed and so they will be assured that our security is protected. I think we should have full answers. That is the reason I put the question forward.
All of a sudden we are faced with a visiting Russian economics professor, and it is stated he is the first Soviet citizen to accept such an assignment in Canada. In view of the stringent control normally exercised by the Russians the question is being asked why

the Russian authorities have permitted this to happen. I know of no announcement that has been made, but perhaps unbeknown to us there may be an exchange program under which our Canadian professors who espouse our social system have been invited to occupy chairs at Soviet universities. Has this happened or is this a one-way traffic? If it is a one-way traffic, what is the thinking of the department in permitting it to take place on this basis?
I have no fear at all as to our present free enterprise social structure being able to stand on its own feet in the full light of any analysis that searching minds and free people want to make. As far as I am concerned, it is the greatest system on earth and it has provided more goods at better prices to more people than any other social system in the world. Therefore I have no fear about its being able to stand on its own feet. But here we have coming to this country a leading Russian professor who subscribes to an alien system which in most cases locks its doors against investigation and interrogation. We are permitting this man to come here. What is his purpose? How far can he go? What freedom is he to be allowed in this assignment? He will be dealing with adolescent minds and great concern is being expressed.
I hope that rather than mere verbiage about how this happened, how the department permitted it and so on we will receive straight answers. If there is something to be gained, if it is a fair exchange, if the Russian people are being placed in the position of being open to receiving answers to their questions from our people in the same way that our people in Canada will be exposed to answers from this Russian professor as a result of his visit, I think this should be known, because it would allay people's fears. I put these questions to the minister's parliamentary secretary and I hope he will be able to answer them completely tonight so that the fears expressed in some of the letters I have already received in this short time will be allayed so far as the action of the federal government in this action is concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF RUSSIAN
subsubtopic: PROFESSOR AT UNIVERSITY OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised many questions and in the three minutes allotted me I doubt very much that I will be able to satisfy him completely. I can say, however, that the hon. member in raising this matter has drawn attention to one particular case in isolation from a num-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ber of considerations. As he is no doubt well aware, for some years it has been the policy of the Canadian government to agree to cultural exchanges between Canada and other countries, including the Soviet union, whenever we were able to secure conditions of reciprocity. This policy is of long standing and has been subject to periodical review under this and previous governments.
In implementing these general policies it should be obvious that in this, as in other fields, officials carry out their responsibilities under general directives laid down by the government. There was no reason why the case to which the hon. member refers should have been brought particularly to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). The matter was dealt with according to established procedure.
The arrangements for this exchange have involved the officials of the Canadian government department concerned, both in Ottawa and in Moscow. No objection was taken to the initiative by the University of Saskatchewan to arrange for Professor Nicolaev to come to Canada. Education is of course a matter of provincial responsibility. The decision to bring Professor Nicolaev to Saskatchewan was taken by the university of that province. In this particular case, there were no reasons for refusing to grant a visa to Professor Nicolaev, provided suitable arrangements had been made, as was the case, by the University of Saskatchewan.
For the hon. member's information, the details of this case are as follows: Toward the end of last year the University of Saskatchewan approached the Soviet ministry of higher education with an invitation to nominate a qualified Soviet economist for a visiting professorship at the university's institute of social sciences for the 1964-65 academic year. In response to this invitation, the Soviet authorities submitted the name of Mr. A. B. Nicolaev of the Moscow state university. The University of Saskatchewan accepted the nomination and requested the Department of External Affairs to expedite the issuance of a visa. As I suggested earlier, this visit should be viewed as part of a developing exchange of visits and contacts between Canada and the Soviet union in the academic field. In the past year or so, arrangements have been made for a number of Canadian students and professional people to work in and visit institutions of learning in the U.S.S.R.
